stories.headline: A flood of woes in Assam
stories.deck: Most people across Assam’s flood-prone districts know what to expect during six rainy months in a year, but the residents of Sivasagar and Charaideo, two historically safer districts along the Assam-Nagaland border, were not prepared for what hit them following a spell of heavy rainfall from July 18 to 22. The scale of devastation that occurred at an unprecedented speed has increased the…
stories.bodyText:
Tamuli Gaon, a village in eastern Assam’s Jorhat district, is about 40 kilometres west of neighbouring Sivasagar district’s Bihubar, the epicentre of destruction by one of Assam’s worst localised floods since the 1950s. The gushing waters that submerged much of Sivasagar and adjoining Charaideo districts on July 19–20 lost momentum by the time they reached the periphery of Tamuli Gaon, but inundated the surrounding, low-lying paddy fields, to turn this village of 110 families into an island.
The village’s Biju Kumar Sarmah, a teacher nicknamed Gospuli for his obsession with plantation drives to “reclaim what’s lost”, explains why Tamuli Gaon was spared. “The water did not have enough force to cut through the embankments in our area, unlike those a few kilometres to the east, toward Sivasagar district,” he says. He is not sure whether the distance from Bihubar would provide Tamuli Gaon with insurance against a bigger disaster, with at least two more months of rain to go this year. “The floodwaters have less than half the distance to travel from Bihubar to Tamuli Gaon than from Mon to Bihubar,” he says.
Mon, the headquarters of Nagaland’s district of the same name, bore the brunt of extremely heavy rainfall that drenched parts of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, and Nagaland from July 18 to 22. The rainfall triggered landslides, killing 11 people in Mon town, and large volumes of water from five major rivers and numerous streams originating in Mon district gushed downstream, carrying earth and debris, to swamp more than 80% of Sivasagar and Charaideo districts.
“The water trickled in gently around noon on July 19. It suddenly became a mahapralay (total destruction), and before we could understand what was happening, we were being thrashed about in neck-deep water,” says Shivraj Sharma of Bihubar Nepalikhuti, a village near the Assam-Nagaland border that was home to some 200 families of mostly dairy farmers.
Nepalikhuti is close to the Dikhow River and along the axis of the road connecting Mon to Naginimora, a border town in Nagaland that thrives on coal mining and trade. Several stretches of this road were almost erased by the overflowing Dikhow.
Sharma and other members of his family clambered atop their tin-roofed house to save themselves, watching helplessly as a few villagers were swept past, flailing their arms to grab anything to anchor them. As the water level kept rising, the Sharma family — drenched from the incessant rainfall and without food for two days — feared meeting a watery grave like their cattle. “Our tethered cows could have survived if we had the time to cut the ropes,” he says.
When the floodwaters receded, Bihubar Nepalikhuti was under at least 4 feet of silt with branches of trees, upturned furniture, household appliances, clothes, books, bags, footwear, utensils, mattresses, and bloated carcasses of livestock sticking out from the surface.
Silt-smeared refrigerators, television sets, two-wheelers, sofa sets, packaged foods, and other items continue to flank a 19-km road from Bihubar to Simaluguri, where floodwaters caused extensive damage to an arterial railway track, snapping train services between eastern Assam and the rest of the State for almost a fortnight.
The road was largely cleared a fortnight later, but most houses and structures on either side continued to be enveloped in debris. Septuagenarian Habibur Rahman recalls a “terrifying sound” as the floodwaters approached their house at Santak Bihubar village, snapping trees and slicing through anything in the way. “I don’t know when we can go back to our house. I no longer have the money and the energy to clear the head-high debris from our house,” he says.
The ordeal has been similar or worse for Moromi Bora Bordoloi of Bihubar Siloni Majgaon, Ranjit Gogoi of Charing Gogoi Ali, Pithuram Konwar of Dighalijan, and Jatin Saikia of Bhitoruwal Gaon. “We were just not prepared, maybe because we are not used to such water fury,” Bordoloi, a weaver-homemaker, says.
ALSO WATCH Watch: Assam floods: is development or climate change to blame? | Above the Fold | Aug 5 2026
Caught unaware
The Sivasagar, Charaideo, and Jorhat district authorities, too, were caught unawares by the deluge. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma, after touring the flood-hit districts, admitted that the administration in each could not mobilise rescue and relief operations for seven days since the disaster struck. He said this was understandable, as these districts do not have a history of major floods and the authorities were not as disaster-ready as other districts that experience floods regularly.
These three districts accounted for 71 of the 99 people who died in the floods across 16 districts from April to August 8, 2026, and more than 94% of some 7.21 lakh flood-affected people. The scale of the disaster across much of the 4,426 sq. km covered by the three districts is perhaps comparable to the 11-day flooding of southern Assam’s Silchar town in June 2022, with water levels rising to 12 feet in some areas. There’s a difference though: Silchar is prone to flooding or water-logging, often fleetingly, unlike Charaideo or Sivasagar.
Disaster management experts explained why the government machinery was underprepared in the three districts. “There’s a flaw in the government’s approach to disaster management, which is to identify risks and concentrate on high-risk areas. The planning needs to change. If low or zero-risk areas become high-risk overnight, there’s very little people can do, as was the case with the three districts,” says Partha Jyoti Das, a climate, water, and disaster specialist with Assam-based biodiversity conservation group Aaranyak. He adds that getting the right people for climate-smart or climate-resilient flood management is crucial. “Ditto with factoring in fluctuating climate change scenarios in everything to minimise disasters.”
According to the 2018 Climate Vulnerability Assessment prepared by the Indian Institute of Technology-Guwahati and IIT-Mandi in collaboration with Bengaluru’s Indian Institute of Science, Assam was the most vulnerable State in the Indian Himalayan region.
The 2021 index of the same assessment ranked Assam, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Bihar as the States most vulnerable to extreme climate events and hydro-meteorological disasters. The index analysed 640 districts in India and found that 463 of these were vulnerable to extreme floods, droughts, and cyclones, and that more than 80% of the country’s population resides in districts highly exposed to climate risks.
Rainfall-induced floods, landslides, and erosion indicate that people in all 35 districts in Assam are highly exposed to climate risks. Often, 25-32 districts experience floods in a year, more severe in districts perched below 88 metres, the average elevation of Sivasagar and Charaideo districts.
This is not unusual. A combination of geography, medium-to-heavy monsoon rainfall for almost six months, and a network of silt-laden rivers has made floods an annual phenomenon in Assam.
Experts say the pattern of flooding changed after the Assam-Tibet earthquake in 1950 triggered massive landslides across the eastern Himalayas, sending large volumes of sediment into the Brahmaputra River and its tributaries and permanently altering the river system.
Deforestation (Assam lost about 3,600 sq. km of tree cover from 2001–2025, accelerating soil erosion and making the rivers shallower with silt), infrastructure push in the geologically young and fragile hills, ageing breach-prone river embankments, and climate change amplified the recurring disaster, often suddenly in specific areas instead of the “laahe-laahe (slow) flooding” of yore.
Hydrologists and disaster specialists are baffled by the ever-changing rainfall pattern, drenching some areas heavily and barely wetting others. For instance, while Sivasagar and Charaideo districts drowned, their western neighbours, the perennially flood-prone Morigaon and Nagaon districts, faced drought-like situations. This, perhaps, explains the monsoon paradox.
According to the India Meteorological Department, Assam recorded a 28% rainfall deficit in June and July, while about 6,500 sq. km area on either side of the Assam-Nagaland border received up to 490% more rainfall than normal, contributing to the floods in Sivasagar and Charaideo.
Mining menace
When India’s National Green Tribunal banned Meghalaya’s hazardous rat-hole coal mining in April 2014, green activists in Assam sought attention to similar, potentially “more dangerous” activities along the State’s borders with Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland. More than a decade ago, Golaghat-based activist Apurba Ballav Goswami said the water bodies in Assam linked to the Nagaland-origin Dikhow, Disang, Jhanji, and Teyap Rivers were turning acidic due to run-off from unscientifically established mines. This, he said, was foreboding for downstream areas in Assam.
A 2018 PIL (public interest litigation) filed by Congress leader Debabarata Saikia, then a Congress MLA from Nazira, in the Gauhati High Court indicated rampant coal mining was not the only source of disaster for Sivasagar and adjoining districts. It conveyed that illegal sand and stone mining and encroachment of fragile river beds were also inviting trouble. The PIL focussed on the Dikhow, Sivasagar’s lifeline-turned-sorrow, seeking an immediate ban on the potentially catastrophic riverbed mining.
Following the court’s directive, the government sent teams from January to March 2019 to verify the allegations, concentrating on Bihubar and adjoining areas near the Assam-Nagaland border. The inquiry revealed eight stone quarries, 81 stone crushers, and the seizure of about 10,000 cubic metres of minor minerals in the area. The report described Bihubar and the surrounding areas as a hub of mining, distribution, supply, and interstate transportation. It also said that most of the gravel and boulders were transported from Nagaland.
Saikia petitioned the High Court again in 2019, arguing that illegal mining was continuing despite the damning government report, which the court had reproduced in its order. The second petition sought a specialised mining task force, a high-powered committee to study the fragile ecosystem of the Dikhow, measures to prevent changes in the river’s course, and a master plan covering illegal mining, bank erosion, drainage, and associated problems.
In October 2019, the court directed the Assam government to constitute a dedicated Mines and Minerals Task Force Battalion and a high-level committee for river conservation, adding that it expected action within three months.
“The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government virtually ignored the directive. Unchecked stone and sand mining in the Dikhow contributed to the extensive soil erosion along its course from Nagaland. The outcome is the ordeal our district went through in July,” Saikia, from oil town Nazira near Sivasagar, says. Nazira is the Assam Asset’s headquarters of ONGC, whose office-residential complex was submerged, forcing many executives to stay in hotels and homestays on higher ground.
Sivasagar MLA and Raijor Dal president Akhil Gogoi was more vocal about the “indiscriminate” coal and stone mining. “Rainwater accumulated in the hollowed coal pits in Nagaland, eventually burst out and caused widespread devastation in Assam,” he says, also pointing to the “rape of the rivers” by the mining mafia. His Sivasagar-based party leader Manas Konwar went a step further, naming two local BJP legislators, one of them a Minister, as the kingpins of the stone and coal mining operations along the Assam-Nagaland border.
After the floods, local YouTubers and reel-makers filmed the mining activities along the border. Some of them showed several earthen roads built across the Dikhow River to facilitate the movement of trucks carrying coal, stone chips, and sand. “Built during the dry season, these roads are like multiple dams that block the water upstream, within Nagaland. The accumulated water swells during the monsoon and cuts through these dams,” a Brahmaputra Board official says, declining to be quoted. The primary role of this Board, under the Ministry of Jal Shakti, is to plan, coordinate, and integrate implementation of measures to control floods, mitigate riverbank erosion, and harness water resources across the northeastern region.
While the Assam Chief Minister, speaking to the media, denied any mining activities in Assam, community-based organisations in Nagaland rejected “theories” that their hill State and their people were responsible for Assam’s floods.
Former Nagaland minister Mmhonlumo Kikon noted reports that Nagaland’s insurgent groups are financially involved in coal mining, and that mining in Nagaland materially caused or intensified the eastern Assam floods. He also said the reports frequently move from allegations, anecdotes, and general environmental risks to an implied conclusion about criminality and flood causation without producing the evidence needed to make that connection. “A clear and thorough report on the investors from Assam or elsewhere, the market where this coal is sold, the number of challans (invoices) issued by the relevant departments in Assam, or even the Assam police record on the trucks transporting the coal would have been helpful,” he says.
Post-flood trauma
Sivasagar was formerly known as Rangpur, the administrative and political capital of the Ahoms, who ruled large swathes of Assam for 600 years until the British took control of the region in the early 1800s. Historians say Sivasagar (Charaideo was carved out of it in August 2015) was strategic for the Ahoms to administer a vast region, and that the region was relatively flood-free compared to the rest of the Brahmaputra Valley. The Ahom royal chronicles refer to flooding in and around the capital at intervals of more than a hundred years, including in 1691 and 1793.
“Sivasagar’s misery indicates that the flood cycle may have reduced (after the last one recorded 60 years ago) and become more catastrophic due to several factors, mostly man-made. The unpredictable climate change scenario is adding to this misery, making old water discharge data on which flood control measures are designed redundant,” says Bibhash Sarma, an engineering teacher and consultant to Assam’s Water Resources Department.
Aaranyak’s Das adds that the ever-changing rainfall pattern is the new normal. “The administrative machinery must understand that no part of Assam or anywhere else in the northeast is safe from floods and associated disasters. Everyone, down to the farmer, needs to be wired to anticipate such calamities during the six rainy months in the region.”
According to disaster watchers, getting the right people for climate-smart or climate-resilient flood management will not be enough to reduce disasters in a State where living with “normal” floods has been a way of life. “Disaster preparedness has to be designed around the realisation that there is not an inch of flood-free land in Assam, and that areas considered zero- or low-risk can become high-risk overnight,” Das says. Others called for surface water management by undoing or minimising the damage done by unscientifically planned roads, flyovers, hydropower, housing, and other infrastructure projects, which have largely claimed wetlands that once acted as water sponges during floods.
The pessimism “unless corrective measures are initiated now” has sunk in among Sivasagar-Charaideo’s flood survivors. Neighbours joked about taking refuge in her house during extreme floods when Lakshmi Devi began constructing her RCC house at Bihubar Nepalikhuti in 2022.
In 2026, more than 60 of them did take refuge on the roof of her house when the “tsunami” struck the village on July 19. “I could not imagine then that the joke would become a reality in less than four years,” she says, mourning the loss of her 10 cows. “I may have to add another floor to our house, but there’s no guarantee that the next flood will not reach the second-floor ceiling,” she adds.
District officials say the challenges in the areas returning to normality include clearing several feet of silt and debris from houses and paddy fields, sanitising the foul-smelling flood-hit areas, and ensuring adequate healthcare for livestock and people vulnerable to water- and vector-borne diseases such as Japanese encephalitis, which claimed 19 lives this year, before the floods.
The biggest challenge could be the trauma of expecting the worst in a State that recorded 160 and 181 human deaths during the 2017 and 2022 floods, respectively. “I don’t think anyone in Jorhat, Sivasagar, or Charaideo can sleep peacefully, at least during the remaining two months of the monsoon this year, if not later,” says Sarmah, whose Tamuli Gaon village is 18 km south of the Brahmaputra. “The Brahmaputra has been a bigger sorrow for Assam than the Dikhow this time, and much closer to us,” he says.

stories.headline: Smaller, leaner GCCs reshape India’s engineering playbook
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 The new global capability centre (GCC) model is increasingly smaller, leaner and engineering-led, with companies building specialised teams around AI and product engineering rather than focusing on scale and headcount.
IT industry body Nasscom’s data shows more than 420 GCCs in India have parent firms with revenues of less than $100 million, pointing to the growing presence of smaller enterprises in the GCC ecosystem. A growing trend favours technology, product development and niche capabilities.
US audio major Bose Professional’s Mangaluru R&D centre illustrates the shift. Focused on next-generation professional audio products, the centre began with one employee, has grown to 25 and is planned to scale up to 75, CEO John Maier told TOI last year. The company is also bringing more product development in-house to improve efficiency and speed of innovation.
Nasscom cited McCain Foods, CoreStack, Blueshift, Veryon, Greenlight and Ava Care as examples of smaller specialised GCCs.
Arindam Sen, GCC sector leader (TMT) at EY India, said smaller GCCs should not be treated as a fundamentally different operating model because of their size. A company with $1 billion in revenue may begin with a 20-, 50- or 100-person GCC, while a $60-billion enterprise may establish a centre with several hundred or even 1,000 employees.
“Headcount alone should not define the category or determine the strategic relevance of a GCC,” Sen said.
What is changing is the nature of work undertaken, with newer centres focused on AI, product engineering, cybersecurity and advanced analytics rather than transactional functions. Access to specialised talent, faster product development, intellectual property ownership and resilience can justify a smaller centre, Sen said.
ANSR founder Lalit Ahuja said AI is reshaping GCC economics, allowing companies to accomplish more with smaller teams. Companies can begin with teams of 20 or fewer focused on specialised capabilities rather than building large workforces upfront.
Some companies are cutting initial workforce assumptions by 30%-50%, with plans that once envisaged 5,000 employees being recalibrated to around 3,000, Ahuja said. Some AI-native GCCs also operate with a permanent core of roughly 50%-70% of their workforce, with the rest supported by flexible talent and service partners.
He said the resulting productivity gains are changing how GCC performance is assessed, with metrics including faster time to market, improved quality and execution, a shrinking technology backlog, fewer software licences, and the ability to take on more high-value work.
Nitika Goel, managing partner at Zinnov, said the sub-$100 million segment is a launchpad rather than a fixed category. On average, companies take six to 10 years to cross $100 million in revenue, but a fast-growing minority in AI, deep-tech and vertical SaaS can grow 40%-70% annually and cross the threshold in two to three years.
That makes headcount an inadequate measure of a centre’s importance, she said.
“What actually matters is value density, whether that team owns a global product or a critical AI capability, and how fast the parent starts routing more strategic work there.”
Goel described the trend as the democratisation of the GCC model, citing RapidAI, Meltwater, Sonatype and Guardant Health. Such centres can become viable within 12-24 months, compared with the traditional three-to-five-year scale-up model.
Sen said ROI should ultimately be linked to outcomes. A product engineering centre could be measured through release velocity, platform adoption, product reliability and revenue impact, while an AI centre could be be assessed on use cases deployed, productivity improvement, adoption and value realised.
“The real question is not whether the centre is large enough, but whether it owns outcomes that matter to the enterprise,” Sen said.

stories.headline: Miscreants pose as prospective tenants, rob woman of gold chain in Bengaluru
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Two men posing as prospective tenants allegedly assaulted a 59-year-old woman and fled with her 40-gram gold mangalya chain in east Bengaluru recently.
According to a complaint filed by Yashoda, a resident of Konadasapura who runs a small shop in front of Safal Market, she was approached by an acquaintance named 
Bharath
 about two weeks ago. Bharath’s parents used to run a roadside eatery on Yashoda’s property and had returned to their native Chintamani. Bharath claimed that he was studying nina college nearby.
Yashoda told 
TOI
, “Bharath told me that two of his friends were looking for a house on rent and they would visit her the following morning to see the property.”
However, no one turned up the next day. A man visited her shop, introducing himself as Bharath’s friend, and enquired about the rent and advance before leaving.
Around 8pm on Aug 5, two men arrived at her house, claiming to be Bharath’s friends, and asked her to show them the house she intended to rent out. Trusting them, Yashoda showed them her the vacant house adjacent to her residence. “The duo complained of cracks in the wall and told me that one of them was bringing his pregnant wife and wanted to fix it,” the complainant said.
“They took some tools from my house, including a hammer, and started hitting the wall. I objected to it and asked them only to clean the house and that they could fix the cracks with paint after shifting. 
Within two minutes, they came to my house while I was cooking. One of them put his hand on my shoulder as if he were a friend. When I retorted, they tried to grab my mangalya chain. I held on to it and tried to escape. But they assaulted me and robbed me of the chain. When they were fleeing, I tried to stop them, but they overpowered me and fled on a bike they had parked nearby,” Yashoda said.
Yashoda told Avalahalli police that she remembered Bharath having said his sister had been married to a nearby villager.
A senior officer said, “We have secured the trio and subjected them to questioning and are making efforts to recover the gold chain. Bharath is the mastermind behind the crime, and the miscreants had followed her for almost two weeks to rob her of valuables.”

stories.headline: Lalbagh walkers continue protest against tunnel road project
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru
: Walkers, residents and activists continued their weekly protest against the proposed tunnel road project by forming a human chain on Lalbagh Rock Sunday. The group plans to hold the demonstration every Sunday until the project is stayed by the high court.
Around 30 people gathered on the rock, voicing concerns over the tunnel’s potential impact on Lalbagh’s ecology and geological heritage, including its billions-of-years-old rock formation.
However, protesters were unable to raise slogans because of restrictions on holding protests at locations other than Freedom Park. Police personnel also asked them not to display banners or placards. Organisers said the restrictions discouraged more people from joining the weekly demonstration.
S Umesh Kumar, president of Lalbagh Walkers’ Association, said ongoing soil testing near the garden’s Siddapura Gate had encountered hard rock at a depth of around 60ft. “The next hearing of the PIL petition filed against the project in the high court is coming up on Aug 20. We expect the court to take cognisance of the project’s impact,” he told 
TOI
.
Activist Vinod Jacob urged more citizens to join such protests, saying the initiative should grow into a citizen-led movement to protect Bengaluru’s environment and remaining green spaces.

stories.headline: Stray dogs in Bengaluru north corporation limits to check-in at new shelter this week
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Bengaluru North City Corporation (BNCC) is set to begin shifting institutional stray dogs to its newly completed shelter at Medi Agrahara this week, with the facility ready to accommodate up to 500 dogs. The Rajasthan-based NGO, Bhootpurva Sainik Welfare Sansthan, has been selected to operate the shelter, built at a cost of Rs 2 crore.
BNCC commissioner Pommala Sunil Kumar said the work order had been issued. “By Wednesday or Thursday, picking up of dogs will start. We are the first corporation to complete a shelter,” he said.
The chief minister is also expected to review the initiative at a meeting scheduled this week, Kumar said. The corporation would closely monitor the shelter’s functioning and would withhold payment if the contractor failed to maintain the required standards.
BNCC’s chief veterinary officer Dr HK Gangadharaiah said the corporation had awarded a one-year contract at Rs 3,050 per dog per month. “We had estimated around 900 institutional dogs in BNCC limits about six months ago. However, some institutions have offered to continue taking care of the dogs on their campuses. 
The Animal Welfare Board of India rules have a provision for this if the institution has more than two acres,” he said.
On concerns over pollution clearances, Gangadharaiah said a team from the pollution control board had visited the shelter, following RTIs filed by citizens, and have not raised any objections.
He said the shelter currently has a 15-foot pit and biomedical waste is being managed through a firm that has an MoU with the adjoining ABC centre. “A BDA layout is coming up nearby. Once the underground drainage is completed, we will connect the shelter to it,” he said.
Apart from institutional dogs, the corporation also plans to pick up aggressive dogs. “It is better to pick up aggressive dogs even from the point of view of their own safety. Recently, there was an instance where a dog was killed by people after a biting incident,” he said.
BNCC is also proposing another 500-dog shelter in Dasarahalli, which will be taken up after the present facility begins functioning.
West shelter waste: KSPCB flags possible Vrishabhavathi discharge
Meanwhile, Karnataka State Pollution Control Board has written to Bengaluru West City Corporation, seeking details of clearances and environmental safeguards for its dog shelter at Sumanahalli, besides information on the quantity of water to be used daily, treatment and disposal of wastewater, and solid waste management.
The board has also raised the possibility of wastewater flowing into Vrishabhavathi river and sought details of measures taken to prevent such discharge.
In its response to an RTI filed by advocate Geetha Misra, KSPCB stated consent to establish, an approved waste disposal plan, consent to operate and other clearances had not been obtained for the shelter.
“Apart from animal welfare, these shelters also pose a threat to human health,” she said, adding the noise generated by the shelters could cause sleep disturbance for nearby residents.

stories.headline: Man held after allegedly assaulting two men with baseball bat in Bengaluru’s AECS Layout
stories.bodyText:
The HAL police on Friday (August 7) arrested a private company employee for allegedly assaulting two men with a baseball bat following a trivial altercation near AECS Layout.
The accused, identified as Arun, a resident of AECS Layout, was let off on station bail. The incident took place on August 6. According to the FIR, the victims, Sandeep Kumar and his friend Rohith, were waiting for another friend to join them for a morning walk near an ice cream parlour in Block A of AECS Layout at around 5 a.m.
Arun allegedly arrived in an SUV at high speed and stopped near the two men. Despite having no prior acquaintance with them, he allegedly asked them whether they were “terrorists”. Rohith responded that they were Indian citizens.
The accused then threatened the duo and demanded that they produce their identity cards. When the two men questioned his authority to seek their IDs, Arun allegedly grew angry, abused them and picked up a baseball bat kept in his car to attack them. When Rohith attempted to record the incident on his phone, Arun allegedly struck the phone with the bat and assaulted the victims, the FIR stated.

stories.headline: Clean power push: India hits 300 GW non-fossil capacity milestone ahead of 2030 target
stories.deck: India has now achieved over 300 GW of non-fossil fuel electricity generation capacity. This significant milestone represents more than half of the nation's total installed power capacity. Solar power leads this expansion, followed by wind and hydro energy sources. The country aims to reach 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by the year 2030. Domestic manufacturing for solar equipment has also seen…
stories.bodyText:
India has crossed 300 GW of installed non-fossil fuel-based electricity generation capacity, reaching more than 60 per cent of its target of 500 GW by 2030, according to the ministry of new and renewable energy.
As of July 31, the country's total non-fossil fuel capacity stood at 300.50 GW, while overall installed electricity generation capacity was around 552 GW.
This means non-fossil sources now account for more than 54 per cent of India's total installed power capacity, the ministry said in a statement.
Solar accounts for more than half of non-fossil capacity
Solar power remains the largest component of India's non-fossil capacity at 164.59 GW, followed by wind power at 58.14 GW and hydro power at 57.24 GW.
The remaining capacity comprises 11.75 GW of bio-power and 8.78 GW of nuclear power.
Solar capacity has increased sharply from 2.8 GW in 2014 to around 165 GW currently.
Wind power capacity has also risen from 21 GW in 2014 to 58.14 GW.
The government said India added a record 55.29 GW of non-fossil fuel-based electricity capacity in 2025-26.
Solar accounted for 44.6 GW of the additions, while wind contributed 6 GW.
Renewable power generation more than doubles
The increase in installed capacity has also been accompanied by higher renewable electricity generation.
According to the ministry, renewable energy generation increased from 190.96 billion units (BU) in 2014-15 to 477.79 BU in 2025-26.
Domestic manufacturing capacity for solar equipment has also expanded. The capacity listed under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) for solar photovoltaic modules has crossed 200 GW, compared with 2.3 GW in 2014.
The ministry attributed the expansion to measures including the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme, which supports domestic manufacturing of high-efficiency solar modules.
India has 200 GW to add by 2030
With non-fossil capacity at 300.50 GW as of July 31, India needs to add roughly 199.5 GW to reach its stated target of 500 GW by 2030.
The ministry said the expansion is also being accompanied by efforts to reduce industrial emissions and develop the green hydrogen sector.
It is implementing the National Green Hydrogen Mission, with the stated aim of developing India as a hub for the production, use and export of green hydrogen and its derivatives.
The latest capacity figures were released by the ministry of new and renewable energy.

stories.headline: '$200 billion market in 15 countries': Here's what India can do if US slaps 100% tariffs
stories.deck: As the US contemplates imposing substantial tariffs on Russian crude, India is strategically exploring alternative markets to bolster its exports. With fifteen potential markets worth an impressive two hundred billion dollars, Indian exporters are adapting to global challenges. In contrast to the US, where merchandise exports reached eighty-seven billion dollars, shipments to alternative…
stories.bodyText:
The US is planning to slap a 100% tariff on Russian crude customers, and concerns are rising over India’s next move.
The Trump administration's green signal for imposing the hefty duty on countries buying Russian crude has raised concerns over India’s exports. However, economist SP Sharma said that Indian exporters have 15 alternative markets for the same products, with a potential $200 billion market waiting beyond the US.
Speaking to ANI, Sharma said India has scope to diversify its exports and is not excessively dependent on the US market, despite the strong trade and economic relationship between the two countries.
"We have another 15 markets where we can export our same products which we are exporting to the US. If the exports to the US are around 87-88 billion dollars in merchandise exports, then we have a large market of 200 billion dollars in another 15 countries in the same products," Sharma said.
Among the markets he identified are the Netherlands, France, the UK, countries in Latin America, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Nepal.
Major market but not the only one
India's merchandise exports to the US increased to $87.3 billion in 2025-26 from $86.5 billion in 2024-25, despite tariff-related uncertainty and other global headwinds, Sharma said.
He said Indian exporters had continued to expand shipments because of demand for Indian products in the US and their competitiveness in labour-intensive goods.
"Despite these headwinds, our exporters were able to show resilience, were able to make increase in their export trajectory because there is a lot of demand in the US for Indian products, we are competitive and we are providing the labour-intensive products to the US," he said.
But the US is not necessarily the fastest-growing destination for Indian exports, according to Sharma. He said shipments to some other markets are expanding at a quicker pace.
"If we are growing with US at 10-15 per cent, then our growth rate in exports with other markets is between 20-25 per cent. So I believe we have alternatives and we are not that much dependent on the US economy," Sharma said.
Higher tariffs could hurt US consumers too
While pointing to alternative markets, Sharma also stressed that India and the US continue to have strong economic ties. The two countries are also engaged in negotiations for a bilateral trade agreement.
He argued that tariffs of up to 100 per cent would not work in favour of either economy, as higher duties on Indian products could push up prices for American consumers. India, he said, is a competitive and low-cost supplier.
"Trade is always for the welfare, trade is not for the tussles," Sharma said.
"Such kind of announcements are not in favour of US economy too because they will face the inflation," he added.
Sharma said continued trade engagement between India and the US would be more beneficial for both economies than imposing additional tariff barriers.

stories.headline: Gold, silver prices may rise next week as US inflation data, Gulf tensions guide markets
stories.deck: Gold and silver prices are expected to remain firm next week. Investors will track inflation data from major economies and West Asia developments. Upcoming Chinese economic data will also be important for industrial metals. Analysts predict gold and silver will trade with a positive bias. Volatility is expected to remain elevated due to economic data and geopolitical uncertainty.
stories.bodyText:
Gold and silver prices are expected to remain firm next week, with inflation data from major economies and developments around efforts to end hostilities in West Asia likely to influence bullion markets, analysts said.
Investors will track inflation figures from the US, Germany, Japan and India. Upcoming Chinese economic data will also be important for industrial metals, according to analysts.
“Gold and silver momentum looks positive and are expected to trade with a positive bias and move up towards Rs 1.57 lakh per 10 grams and Rs 2.80 lakh per kg in the short term,” Pranav Mer, senior vice president, EBG - commodity & currency research, JM Financial Services Ltd, said, as quoted by news agency PTI.
Gold, silver post sharp weekly gains
On the domestic market, gold futures for October delivery rose Rs 8,444, or nearly 6 per cent, during the week to close at Rs 1.51 lakh per 10 grams.
Silver futures for September delivery gained Rs 14,268, or nearly 7 per cent, to settle at Rs 2.31 lakh per kg on the Multi Commodity Exchange.
“Gold witnessed a strong rally this week, gaining nearly 6 per cent, as weaker-than-expected US labour market data revived expectations of a more accommodative monetary policy from the Federal Reserve,” Jateen Trivedi, VP research analyst, commodity and currency, LKP Securities, said, as per PTI.
He added that a weaker US dollar encouraged fresh buying in precious metals and helped gold record one of its strongest weekly gains in recent months.
In international markets, gold futures for December delivery jumped $292.7, or 7 per cent, during the week to finish at $4,399.7 per ounce.
Silver futures for September delivery rose $5.71, or nearly 10 per cent, to $63.50 per ounce.
US data, Iran developments to influence bullion
Mer said gold broke out of its recent consolidation range, supported by a reversal in the US dollar and crude oil prices remaining in corrective mode, with oil falling close to $75 per barrel.
The next set of US inflation data will be closely watched for clues about the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook. Inflation figures from Germany, Japan and India are also due, while Chinese economic data could influence industrial metals.
Developments involving the US and Iran will also remain a key factor for bullion markets, Trivedi said. Any unexpected diplomatic or military announcement could trigger sharp moves in gold and silver when markets reopen on Monday.
“Overall, volatility is expected to remain elevated in the coming week. The combination of US economic data, Federal Reserve expectations, and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty is likely to keep gold highly reactive,” he said.
In the short term, analysts expect gold and silver to retain a positive bias, although their movement is likely to remain sensitive to economic data, interest-rate expectations, currency movements and developments in West Asia.

stories.headline: Crude, Hormuz & more: What will drive stock market this week
stories.deck: This week, Dalal Street will closely observe global geopolitical shifts and local economic data. Investors will pay attention to fluctuations in crude oil prices and news from the Strait of Hormuz. In addition, important domestic inflation figures and updates on foreign exchange reserves are on the horizon. The Q1 FY27 earnings season is set to pick up pace with numerous company results.
stories.bodyText:
After ending the previous week in green, Dalal Street is set to take cues from a mix of global geopolitical developments and key domestic economic indicators in the upcoming trading sessions. This week, investors will closely watch crude oil prices, developments around the Strait of Hormuz and inflation data.
The market will also track foreign portfolio investor (FPI) flows and the progress of the Q1 FY27 earnings season, while developments involving Iran and the broader situation in the Middle East could influence sentiment.
"Domestically, investors will closely monitor the July CPI inflation print, WPI inflation, and the latest foreign exchange reserves data for fresh insights into inflation trends and external sector stability. The Q1 FY27 earnings season will gather further momentum, with several companies, including HAL, Bharat Forge, Grasim Industries, and Tata Motors, scheduled to announce their quarterly results," Ajit Mishra – SVP, Research, Religare Broking Ltd, told PTI.
India's July CPI inflation data is scheduled for release on August 12, followed by WPI inflation data on August 14. Investors will also get the latest foreign exchange reserves data, adding to the domestic macroeconomic indicators due to be monitored during the week.
The US will also release key inflation readings, with CPI and PPI data due on August 12 and 13, respectively.
"The week will also be important from a macroeconomic perspective, with India scheduled to release CPI inflation on August 12 and WPI inflation on August 14. In the US, CPI and PPI (Producer Price Index) data will be released on August 12 and 13, respectively," Santosh Meena, Head of Research at Swastika Investmart Ltd, said.
Hormuz, crude prices key global triggers
Developments around the Strait of Hormuz are likely to remain a major focus for investors, alongside crude oil price movements and negotiations involving Iran.
"Attention will remain firmly focused on the Middle East, where negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz remain fluid," said Ponmudi R, CEO - Enrich Money.
"This week is likely to be shaped by two dominant themes: developments in the Middle East and the July US inflation report. Attention will remain firmly focused on the Middle East, where negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz remain fluid," Ponmudi R, CEO - Enrich Money, an online trading and wealth tech firm, said.
Mishra said global market participants would continue to watch the situation around the Strait of Hormuz, crude oil movements and wider geopolitical negotiations involving Iran.
Globally, the July US inflation report is expected to be the key macroeconomic event this week, while crude oil is another important monitorable for Indian markets.
FPIs remain buyers
Against this backdrop, foreign portfolio investors continued their buying activity in Indian equities. FPIs invested Rs 12,921 crore in Indian stocks during the first week of August.
The buying comes after Indian benchmark indices closed the previous week with gains. The BSE benchmark Sensex advanced 404.53 points, or 0.51 per cent, while the NSE Nifty gained 187.05 points, or 0.76 per cent.
The previous week also saw the rollout of the new Closing Auction Session (CAS) framework for F&O stocks, along with the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy decision and continued geopolitical uncertainties.
"Markets ended the week with modest gains despite heightened volatility, as investors navigated the roll-out of the new Closing Auction Session (CAS) framework for F&O stocks, the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy decision, and lingering geopolitical uncertainties," Mishra said.
Meena said the introduction of the Closing Auction Session was the key highlight of the previous week as it marked the first week under the new system.
With domestic and US inflation readings due this week, crude oil movements, Middle East developments, FPI activity and quarterly earnings are set to provide several triggers for the market.

stories.headline: IPO bonanza: 5 firms to raise over Rs 7,400 crore this week
stories.deck: A bustling week looms for India's primary market as five companies gear up to unveil their IPOs, collectively aiming to gather an impressive Rs 7,443 crore for diverse corporate initiatives. Dhoot Transmission and Molbio Diagnostics set to kick off on August 10, while Milky Mist Dairy Food and Shiprocket will make their appearances later in the week.
stories.bodyText:
India's primary market is heading into a packed week, with five companies set to tap investors through initial public offerings worth a combined Rs 7,443 crore. The line-up includes Dhoot Transmission, Molbio Diagnostics, Milky Mist Dairy Food, Shiprocket and Behari Lal Engineering. The companies will open their issues between August 10 and August 12.
Dhoot Transmission and Molbio Diagnostics will be the first to hit the market on August 10. Milky Mist Dairy Food will follow on August 11, while Shiprocket and Behari Lal Engineering will open their issues on August 12.
The funds raised through the five offerings are largely earmarked for expansion, capital expenditure, repayment of debt and other corporate purposes.
With these five issues, the number of companies launching their IPOs this year will rise to 47. Meanwhile, the maiden public offerings of KKR-backed LEAP India and Technocraft Ventures are currently open for subscription.
The IPO pipeline is also set to remain active, with Blackstone-backed Horizon Industrial Parks, Gaja Capital-backed firm and Shankesh Jewellers, among others, currently expected to announce their IPO price bands next week.
Dhoot Transmission, Molbio open on August 10
Dhoot Transmission will offer its shares in the price range of Rs 829-871 apiece through an IPO worth Rs 3,067 crore.
The offering consists of a fresh issue of up to Rs 1,400 crore, while promoters BC Asia Investments XV Ltd, an entity of Bain Capital, and Mangalam Capital Private Ltd will sell up to 1.91 crore shares through an offer for sale.
Molbio Diagnostics, the Goa-based point-of-care diagnostics company backed by Temasek and Motilal Oswal Private Equity, has set a price band of Rs 768-807 per share for its Rs 904-940 crore IPO.
Its issue includes a fresh issue of up to Rs 200 crore and an OFS of up to 91.66 lakh shares.
The company has also drawn an investment from the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the private-sector investment arm of the World Bank Group. IFC has invested Rs 20 crore as an anchor investor in Molbio, marking its return to India's mainboard IPO market after five years.
IFC's previous investment in a mainboard IPO was in June 2021, when it invested Rs 10 crore as an anchor investor in Dodla Dairy.
Molbio has also seen secondary share transactions involving leading AIFs and institutional investors worth Rs 160 crore, at Rs 807 per share, which is the upper end of its IPO price band.
Among these transactions, 360 ONE Asset invested Rs 30 crore. 3P Investment Managers, Neo Alternative Asset Managers, Kotak Mahindra Life Insurance and Susquehanna International Group invested Rs 25 crore each. WhiteOak Capital Asset Management invested Rs 20 crore, while Motilal Oswal Asset Management invested Rs 10 crore.
Milky Mist IPO
Milky Mist Dairy Food is set to enter the market on August 11 with a Rs 1,553-crore IPO. The company has fixed the price band at Rs 133-140 per share.
The issue will comprise a fresh issue of up to Rs 1,428 crore and an OFS of up to Rs 125 crore. It will be the largest IPO by an Indian dairy company.
Shiprocket, Behari Lal Engineering to follow
Shiprocket will also seek to raise funds from the public market, with its Rs 1,617.5-crore IPO opening on August 12.
The e-commerce enablement platform has fixed the price band at Rs 92-97 per share. Its IPO consists of a fresh issue of up to Rs 885.50 crore and an OFS of up to Rs 732 crore by existing shareholders, including Lightrock, Tribe Capital and Moore Strategic Ventures.
Also opening on August 12 will be Behari Lal Engineering, which is looking to raise Rs 302 crore.
The engineering castings and alloy steel products manufacturer has set a price band of Rs 271-285 per share. The IPO comprises a fresh issue of up to Rs 93 crore and an OFS of up to 73.20 lakh shares by existing shareholders.

stories.headline: Pant — an enigma at the crossroads
stories.deck: Having been replaced as India’s Test vice-captain, he can focus on his primary disciplines without having to attend lengthy team discussions or the distraction of being pulled in different directions; the team needs the most potent version of the player to come to the fore
stories.bodyText:
When we talk one-format India internationals in the current milieu, almost all the focus is on India’s two immediate all-format past skippers. Since May 2025, when they bid adieu to Test cricket within weeks of each other, Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli play for the country only in One-Day Internationals, having already announced their retirement from T20Is at the conclusion of a triumphant World T20 campaign in Bridgetown in June 2024.
There has been so much talk about whether one, or both, or neither, will be present at next year’s 50-over World Cup in southern Africa that most other issues have been relegated to the background. Including the fact that there is another high-profile one-format-only international in recent times, a young man who has completed a decade in India colours but is now at a tenuous crossroads after an eminently forgettable last few months.
As India embarked on a journey of transition, replete with excitement and promise, last summer through a five-Test tour of England, it was expected that the future would be shaped by two of the most luminous gems in the Indian firmament. Shubman Gill’s elevation to the Test captaincy was no surprise, even though he didn’t have a great deal of leadership experience at the First Class level. Gill had time on his side, he was even then one of the top batters whose place wasn’t under threat, and he had shown himself to be a quick learner. Thrust into the role of his deputy was a once-fearless force of nature who had been forced by circumstances to temper his exuberance, both because of extraneous pressure and owing to the fact that, having established himself as one of the seniors within the setup, he had to strike a fine balance between carefree and careless batsmanship.
Rishabh Pant’s rise as the vice-captain of the Test side was welcomed with as much breathless anticipation as Gill’s to the captaincy. Or Pant’s arrival at the batting crease, if you like. With the chunky left-hander, you still don’t know what to expect. Or maybe you do, but even so, what he does simply blows your mind. Pant isn’t reckless; he isn’t someone who doesn’t not put a price on his wicket, though from time to time, ‘Stupid, stupid, stupid’ will surface because that’s just who he is. Successive coaches, from Ravi Shastri to Rahul Dravid to now Gautam Gambhir, have given him the licence to be himself with the rider that he should be a little more selective, a little more game-aware, a little more respectful of situations and conditions.
It might have been tough for Gambhir to reconcile, for instance, to Pant’s extravagant aerial drive to his fifth delivery, from off-spinner Ramesh Mendis, that nestled in long-off’s hands at the NCC ground on Saturday in India’s only practice game, against a Sri Lanka Cricket XI. Most other batters would have been happy to play themselves in, get some circulation going, get a feel of the conditions, prepare conservatively for the two-Test series beginning in Galle next Saturday. But Pant isn’t most people, and that’s precisely what makes him the compelling attraction in front of the stumps that he has been since his Test debut in August 2018.
Pant fell just two balls after attempting a similar stroke that fell just beyond the reach of the backtracking mid-off fielder, compelling Mendis and skipper Sonal Dinusha to push Nishan Madushka back. Perhaps in a show of bravado, or more likely because he backed himself to middle the ball turning away from him and comfortably clear the fielder, Pant went through with the stroke only to put the ball up in the air for Madushka to complete a smart grab. Two runs from five deliveries isn’t what Pant, or the leadership group of Gill and Gambhir would have hoped for, but as mentioned earlier, India have been willing to accept the trade-off because when Pant gets going, the destruction he can wreak is beyond parallel.
Pant’s dalliance with the vice-captaincy didn’t last too long, the decision-makers arriving at the conclusion that he and Indian cricket would be better off without additional responsibilities being thrust on his shoulders. In his first sojourn as Gill’s deputy, Pant was a runaway success. His batting in England, on admittedly excellent tracks for batting, was a sight for sore eyes. While Gill was wooing and wowing the connoisseurs with his correctness and his silken stroke-making on his way to 754 extraordinary runs, Pant was at his innovative, unpredictable best without compromising on consistency. In Leeds during the first Test, he became the first Indian stumper to notch up twin hundreds in England, backed it up with 25 and 65 in the series-levelling win in Birmingham, produced efforts of 74 and 9 in the Lord’s loss and won himself a few million more fans by coming out to bat with a broken foot in the first innings and making a stirring 54 in the fourth Test in Manchester.
On-field heroism
The manner in which he contracted that injury, and the events that followed as he took on-field heroism to a different level, are archetypal Pant. The 28-year-old attempted a reverse against seamer Chris Woakes and only managed to play the ball on to his foot, carried off the field as that part of his body swelled up dramatically within seconds of the impact. When he came out to bat, hobbling and unable to put any weight on his right foot, he still found enough timing and power to smack fours – and a six – as he brought up his fifty to raucous applause and walked off to warm appreciation and genuine respect from England’s fielders.
That broken foot not only ended his England tour but also kept him out of the home series against West Indies in October. By this time, Pant was clearly only in the running for Test matches. His last ODI was in August 2024, his last T20I a week before that, both in Sri Lanka in Gambhir’s first assignment as Dravid’s successor. Sanju Samson and Ishan Kishan in the shorter white-ball format, and K.L. Rahul and Kishan in the 50-over version, have surged well clear in the wicketkeeper-batter stakes, which means the only canvas available to Pant, apart from the IPL which hasn’t been his happiest hunting ground, is the five-day spectacle.
Pant’s return to Test cricket, against South Africa in Kolkata in November, was anything but auspicious as India failed to hunt down 124 on an Eden minefield. Gill’s batting efforts in that Test were restricted to just three deliveries in the first innings as he retired hurt with a neck injury, an affliction that kept him out of the second Test in Guwahati and thrust Pant into the Test skipper’s role for the first time.
Hard times
It was a disastrous initiation; Pant himself played one of the most horrendous strokes of his career, a little after lunch on day three, then oversaw a 408-run hammering – India’s heaviest by runs in Test history. A few months later came a campaign of gigantic failure in the IPL when, under Pant, Lucknow Supergiants hurtled from one misadventure to another. Even before the tournament had ended, Pant had stepped down as captain, and a few weeks later, it was confirmed that the IPL’s most expensive player would return to his original franchise, Delhi Capitals, after taking a heavy pay cut.
Pant had a reasonably fruitful outing in the one-off Test against Afghanistan in New Chandigarh in June, with a somewhat restrained 81 in his, and India’s, only innings of the game that they bossed all the way through. By then, though, he had been replaced as vice-captain by K.L. Rahul, one of the few individuals to have captained the country in all three formats, all in a stand-in capacity. It was the clearest indication that Agarkar’s panel, if no one else, believed that Pant himself and the team as a whole would be better off if he was divested of official leadership responsibilities, though given his standing in the international circuit, Pant can’t not be a leader in his own right.
Now, Pant can focus on his primary disciplines without having to attend lengthy team discussions or the distraction of being pulled in different directions, an inevitable fallout of additional role thrusts. Behind the stumps, he is unconventional and unorthodox, more Mahendra Singh Dhoni than Syed Kirmani or Nayan Mongia. In front of it, he is evidently in a league of his own. Like he showed on Sunday in Colombo, he can stonewall if so required – though even he will admit that he took it too far – and switch gears around his stonewalling without warning. It is exactly this unpredictability that makes him such an irascible force, a revolving door that can exasperate as much as it can exhilarate.
Impressive numbers
Despite the presence in the squad, and possibly in the playing XI, of Dhruv Jurel, there is not even an artificial threat to Pant’s presence in the Test scheme of things. After all, we are talking about someone who averages 43.37 from an even 50 Tests, at a jaw-dropping strike-rate of 74.05 embellished by eight centuries and 19 fifties in 87 innings. These are numbers that would do several specialist batters proud – remember that Mike Atherton and the recently retired Ajinkya Rahane both averaged less than 40 – and yet, there is more to Pant. Such as 162 catches and 16 stumpings, and the very rare ability to change the course of even Test matches with two hours of unadulterated mayhem.
Six of Pant’s eight centuries have come away from home – four in England, and one each in Australia and South Africa – though like most of the rest of his colleagues, he hasn’t played a Test match in Sri Lanka yet. In some ways, the conditions there will be strikingly similar to India, but in others, they won’t be, especially when it comes to pace off the surface. Galle from Saturday, and the SSC ground the week thereafter, will ask questions of Pant that he hasn’t been asked too often in the past, but knowing him, he will find the answers. How he uses those answers, however, will make for fun viewing, as much as how much and how freely he is allowed to use them. There is no point asking Pant to bat like Ravindra Jadeja because, well, he wouldn’t be Pant then, would he? India need the most potent version of Pant to come to the fore. Only a really brave or stupid individual will bet against that eventuating.

stories.deck: “He got kicked,” Carrick told ‌reporters ⁠of Mount, who has played sparingly due ⁠to various injuries since joining the club from Chelsea in 2023
stories.bodyText:
Manchester United manager Michael Carrick played down concerns over Mason Mount after the England midfielder was forced off with an injury during Saturday's 1-1 pre-season draw with Paris St Germain, saying the club had taken a cautious approach.
Mount, 27, was forced off inside 20 minutes in Gothenburg after appearing to suffer a foot injury following a challenge during the friendly, with Tyler Fletcher replacing the midfielder.
"He got kicked," Carrick told reporters of Mount, who has played sparingly due to various injuries since joining the club from Chelsea in 2023.
"We just wanted to be careful and look after him. We've been lucky with injuries so far, so we wanted to be careful."
United trailed 1-0 after Ibrahim Mbaye's opener inside two minutes for PSG, but Bryan Mbeumo levelled before halftime to earn Carrick's side a draw.
Carrick said he was encouraged by his side's performance against the French champions.
"The things that we were trying to get out of the game, a lot of it was there," the 45-year-old told the club's television channel.
"It's good sometimes that the boys have to problem-solve and find their way a little bit. We don't want to always give them the answers, when we don't have to.
"It prepares them a little bit for the season as well. In that respect, there are a lot of things people don't always see that we were quite happy with. There were some good signs there."
United begin their Premier League campaign against promoted Hull City on August 22 after friendlies against Leeds United and AC Milan.

stories.headline: ​Podium finish: On India at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games
stories.deck: India’s women boxers were the highlight of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games
stories.bodyText:
In the truncated Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, India performed well, exceeding expectations and retaining fourth place behind developed nations such as Australia, England, and Canada, despite a sharp drop in medals from 61 to 39, including 13 gold, 17 silver, and nine bronze. The gold rush on the penultimate day, powered by the spectacular performance of the boxers who won seven gold and three silver medals, improved India’s position. While some weight classes had weaker draws, several categories posed strong challenges. Propelled by determination and hard work, five women boxers — Sakshi Chaudhary, Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Priya Ghanghas, and Arundhati Choudhary — and two men, Sachin Siwach and Ankush Panghal, ensured India’s best-ever showing of 10 medals, three more than that in the last edition. The women boxers’ fearless approach established them as a force to reckon with. India won 16 medals in athletics and para-athletics, with notable contributions from para-athletes Dilip Gavit, Soman Rana, and Sharmila Dhankar. In world-class fields, the country’s athletes won 10 medals compared to eight in Birmingham 2022. Neeraj Chopra recovered from injury to take a creditable silver and lead the country to twin-medal glory in javelin along with Yashvir Singh and underlined India’s rising status as a javelin powerhouse. Other moments to cherish included triple jumpers Praveen Chithravel and Selva Prabhu’s twin podium finishes, Gulveer Singh becoming the first Indian to medal in 5000m and 10000m, Murali Sreeshankar winning his second straight long jump silver, Tejaswin Shankar claiming the country’s first-ever decathlon medal, and Sarvesh Kushare pocketing a high jump silver.
Asmita Dey and Harsh Singh sprang a surprise by winning the country’s first gold medals in judo, while Mirabai Chanu lived up to her billing to clinch her third successive gold medal. She led Indian lifters to a significant haul of eight medals. The country’s strong show, against an expectation of around 30 medals, helped the contingent leave Glasgow on a high as Ahmedabad prepares to host a bigger Games offering more medals in 2030. Indian athletes’ praiseworthy performance in Glasgow has raised hopes for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games next month, where a bigger haul is expected from a wider range of disciplines. While India is capable of securing impressive medal collections at the Commonwealth and Asian Games, it needs to raise its level manifold to be counted among the best globally. Aspiring to host the 2036 Olympics, it must identify priority sports and invest in them to ensure a higher finish, even while waging a perennial war against doping.

stories.headline: Fernandez secures dominant British MotoGP victory, Martin extends championship lead
stories.deck: The victory was Raul Fernandez’s second in MotoGP and his first since last ‌year’s Australian Grand Prix, completing an impressive recovery from a ‌crash ⁠in Saturday’s sprint
stories.bodyText:
Trackhouse Racing's Raul Fernandez led from the opening lap to win the British MotoGP on Sunday, capitalising on an early setback for championship leader Jorge Martin at Silverstone.
Spaniard Fernandez swept past pole-sitter Martin into Turn One and never looked back, stretching his advantage to more than four seconds before taking the chequered flag 2.54 seconds clear.
The victory was the Spaniard's second in MotoGP and his first since last year's Australian Grand Prix, completing an impressive recovery from a crash in Saturday's sprint.
"I am really happy for the team. Yesterday I was quite frustrated after my mistake. But we are human, and it is part of the sport," Fernandez said. Spain's Martin, who won the sprint, was hampered at the start when his ride-height device failed to disengage at Turn One, dropping him behind Marc Marquez and fellow Aprilia rider Marco Bezzecchi.
The championship leader recovered to reclaim second from Bezzecchi on lap nine but was unable to get close enough to challenge Fernandez.
Martin's runner-up finish extended his championship lead to 31 points, with Bezzecchi, who finished third, moving up to second in the standings. Ogura lost ground after his first retirement of the season, falling 37 points behind Martin.
"The results here are a big boost of confidence for me and the team," Martin said. "It seems like we found a bit of direction to get the momentum on our side now. The race was fantastic. I made a small mistake at the start, but I am glad I was able to fight back."
Defending world champion Marc Marquez endured another difficult afternoon, finishing seventh after starting sixth on the grid and dropping to fourth in the standings.
Bezzecchi faced stiff competition from Gresini Racing's Alex Marquez, who made a late mistake and dropped back. Alex Marquez continued to put pressure on Bezzecchi, but was unable to chase him down as the Aprilia rider finished third to secure his second podium of the weekend. The result was particularly significant for Bezzecchi, who led the championship earlier this season and was recording his first Sunday finish since winning his home Italian Grand Prix at the end of May.
Alex Marquez came fourth, KTM's Pedro Acosta fifth and VR46 Racing's Fabio Di Giannantonio sixth.

stories.headline: India coach Park reaping the rewards of hard work
stories.deck: For Park Tae-Sang, it is not just a fortnight of good results. It offers a glimpse of his work that he has been putting in Indian badminton, building players who, he hopes, can become the next generation of Indian stars
stories.bodyText:
Two Super 300 titles. Two different players. Two consecutive weeks.
For Park Tae-Sang, it is not just a fortnight of good results. It offers a glimpse of his work that he has been putting in Indian badminton, building players who, he hopes, can become the next generation of Indian stars.
Last Sunday, 17-year-old Tanvi Sharma won the Taipei Open. Seven days later, 26-year-old Ashmita Chaliha made a stunning comeback from a career-threatening knee injury to win the Korea Masters.
"It’s been an amazing two weeks. Last week, Tanvi was also amazing. She is only 17 and won her first BWF-level title. Today, I was even happier because it was Ashmita’s first final and she won the title. As a coach, I’m really happy," Park told PTI from Asan, Korea.
Park spent four years with PV Sindhu in Hyderabad, a stint that culminated in the Tokyo Olympics bronze medal.
After that association ended, he was approached by the Badminton Association of India about working with younger players.
"When I started working with Sindhu, she was already a world champion and had a group of good senior players around her. This time, I thought to myself, ‘Okay, let’s start from the beginning. I will build these players myself, with my own hands.
"The idea was to create a new generation of Indian players." Bigger goal is Olympic qualifying race for 2028 LA Games ========================================== Three years in National Centre of Excellence, Guwahati and the results are beginning to show. However, Park sees the two titles as stepping stones to bigger achievements.
"I think winning two BWF 300-level titles in the last two weeks is a good achievement, but they are only 300-level tournaments. The players are now looking towards the 500, 750 and 1000-level tournaments," he said.
"Our bigger goal is the same for both Tanvi and Ashmita. From May 1 next year, the Olympic qualifying race for the 2028 Los Angeles Games will begin, so next year is going to be very important.
"We will start playing more 500-level tournaments, and they can also play 750-level tournaments. After today’s result, Ashmita’s world ranking should improve enough for her to enter some of those tournaments." For Tanvi and Ashmita to genuinely challenge for an Olympic place, it's a tough road ahead.
“Yeah, 100 per cent. We will try. But we already have some very good players. Sindhu and Unnati (Hooda) are there, right? It will be very tough.” The emphasis, however, remains on development rather than a wholesale change in approach.
"I don’t want to change my training style. Now Ashmita and Tanvi have to follow my instructions and train very hard. I will take care of their endurance and their mental strength. They also need more on-court speed training. These are the areas where I think they need to improve.”
Look at An Se-young
Park also holds up world No. 1 An Se-young as the benchmark for the younger Indian players.
"Actually, An Se-young is at another level. I tell my players that she should be their target. They have to aim for that level.
"Look at An Se-young. She keeps winning 750 and 1000-level tournaments. Look at her mentality and look at her physical strength. Both are really, really strong. So I tell my players, ‘You have to target all of that. You have to learn from her level.’ Tanvi and Ashmita have talent but need to learn how to manage the moments when momentum changes, he said.
"They sometimes take a big lead and then suddenly make an easy service mistake or an easy net mistake... At that time, I have to shout a little more, be stronger with them, and tell them to calm down.
"I always tell ‘Aaramse'. You are doing well. Why are you rushing yourself? Why are you putting so much pressure on yourself to finish the point quickly?’ ‘Calm down. Aaramse.’ It’s an Indian Hindi word, and sometimes I think it is a very good word for them." Now, players such as Devika Sihag, Unnati, Tanvi, Ashmita and others are pushing one another, creating the kind of competitive environment Park believes can accelerate development.
"I think this is a very good system and a very good motivation for the players. Before, there were only a few Indian women’s singles players, mainly Sindhu and Saina.
"This year, Devika won the Thailand Masters. At that time, I told Tanvi and Ashmita, ‘Look at Devika. She worked very hard, trained very hard and finally won the title. So what are you doing? What are you doing now?’" he said.
"Of course, they also have the ability to win titles. But sometimes they train a little harder for a period and then relax. Their movement becomes loose and they lose that intensity. That is when I have to shout at them. I tell them, ‘You don’t have time now to relax when you are a little tired. You have to push more. You have to work harder.”
India's future is strong in singles
Park's confidence in the depth emerging from India's system extends beyond his two latest winners.
"I think the future of Indian badminton is very good. Last year, in the Asian junior championships, India won both the girls’ singles titles at the Under-17 and Under-15 levels. So I think the junior and younger players in India are doing very well. The future is very strong.”
“I want to thank the BAI and the NCE because they are supporting Ashmita, Tanvi and also Ronak Chauhan in men’s singles. He won a bronze medal at the US Open and he is also my player,” he signed off.
